6. Discussion and limitations

At this size the quantum method does not improve on cheap classical baselines. Three observations are worth stating. First, the approximation ratio is not monotone in depth: p = 3 is worse than p = 2 on both systems, although a deeper circuit can represent every state that a shallower one can. This points to the optimiser: with a limited number of iterations from random starting angles, COBYLA does not find the optimal angles for the larger parameter space. Second, the probability of sampling the optimal cut is small and falls steeply with system size (0.149 for 9 buses and 0.0037 for 14), which is what limits the use of QAOA as a sampler. Third, the islanding objective is harder for QAOA than MaxCut because of its constraint and the unbalanced terms; the expected cost remained close to that of a random split while a single-flip descent found the optimum.

The comparison is deliberately in favour of the quantum method in one respect: the simulation is exact, with no shot noise or hardware noise. On hardware the results would be worse. It is deliberately unfavourable in another: the classical optimiser and the number of restarts were not tuned, and better optimisers or parameter initialisation could improve the QAOA numbers.

Limits of the study. Larger networks (30 buses and more), tensor-network simulation, noise models, other optimisers and hardware data were not evaluated; the 30-bus case would need 2^30 amplitudes and was not run. Two systems are a small sample. The weights come from one operating point of each case. The islanding objective is a simplified one that ignores voltage, frequency and protection constraints.
7. Conclusion

On the IEEE 9-bus and 14-bus systems, QAOA simulated exactly reached approximation ratios of 0.71 to 0.82 for flow-weighted MaxCut, whereas greedy search found the optimum, and for islanding its expected cost stayed close to that of random splits. At this size QAOA does not improve on cheap classical baselines, and the classical optimiser rather than the circuit depth appears to be the limit.
Implementation and reproducibility

The study is implemented in research/s_iqicsa_qgrid (exact state-vector QAOA, the classical baselines and the evaluation); a TRL 4 scaffold of the partitioning framework is kept in a separate private repository (articles-qgrid-part). Unit tests on synthetic graphs check the QAOA energy and the baselines. The result file holds the numbers of Table 1.

blocks.x: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Intervals for Binding-Affinity Predictions: Global versus Mondrian Conformal Calibration on EGFR
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Reliable use of machine-learning predictions in drug discovery requires an estimate of how far a predicted binding affinity can be trusted. We add distribution-free uncertainty intervals to the affinity predictions of a hybrid quantum–classical drug-discovery platform, treating the platform's predictor as a black box. Split conformal prediction gives intervals with a guaranteed marginal coverage, and a Mondrian variant calibrates separately within strata of the predicted value. We evaluated both on 3,884 EGFR molecules with measured activity from ChEMBL, using ten random seeds and both random and scaffold-based splits, for a nominal coverage of 0.90. Coverage was 0.896 (95% interval ± 0.009) for a random split and 0.894 (± 0.014) when whole chemical scaffolds were held out, so the marginal guarantee held under chemical-series shift. The Mondrian variant did not improve it: worst-stratum coverage was 0.870 against 0.868 for the global variant on a random split. Coverage within groups of true activity was weaker, with the worst group at 0.83 for a random split and 0.78 for the scaffold split for both variants, and the intervals were wide (about 2.8 pIC50 units, 3.3 under scaffold shift). We report this as a negative result for stratification and a caution for activity-conditional claims. The study uses one target and a random-forest stand-in for the platform's predictor; a second target and the platform's own predictor were not evaluated.
Keywords: conformal prediction; binding affinity; uncertainty quantification; ChEMBL; drug discovery
1. Introduction

A predicted binding affinity is useful in drug discovery only if the user knows how far to trust it. Chemists use predictions to rank molecules for synthesis and testing, and the cost of a wrong ranking is the loss of weeks of laboratory work. Most affinity predictors return a single number, and the error estimates that accompany them are either absent or derived from assumptions, such as Gaussian residuals, that are rarely checked. A quantum–classical drug-discovery platform adds a further reason for caution: its predictor may be a complex pipeline whose error behaviour is not known in advance.

Conformal prediction gives intervals that are valid in finite samples without assumptions about the predictor or the data distribution, provided the calibration and test molecules are exchangeable (Vovk et al., 2005; Lei et al., 2018; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). It can be wrapped around any model, which suits a platform whose predictor is treated as a black box. Two practical questions arise. First, does the guarantee survive the situation in which a model is used: new molecules from chemical series that were not in the training data? In drug discovery this is the rule rather than the exception. Second, an interval that is valid on average may be too narrow for some molecules and too wide for others; does calibrating separately for strata of the predicted value (a Mondrian approach) repair this?

We study both questions on a real target, the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), with measured activities from ChEMBL. We compare global and Mondrian split-conformal intervals under random splits and under splits that hold out whole Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and we also look at coverage within groups defined by the true activity. The answers are partly negative, and we report them as such.
2. Related work

Uncertainty quantification for molecular property prediction has used ensembles, Bayesian approximations and, more recently, conformal prediction. The reliability of a prediction is known to depend on its similarity to the training set: the closer a molecule is to the training data, the more accurate the prediction (Sheridan et al., 2004), and the idea of an applicability domain formalises this (Netzeva et al., 2005). Conformal prediction has been applied to drug–target interaction and affinity prediction in several recent studies, so the novelty of the method is limited; our searches found no study that reports, with ten seeds and confidence intervals, how global and Mondrian calibration compare on a ChEMBL target under both random and scaffold splits, but the search was not exhaustive.

Mondrian conformal prediction calibrates separately within categories and provides category-wise validity (Vovk et al., 2005). The choice of categories is the crux: categories defined by the predicted value are available at test time, whereas categories defined by the true activity are not, and the guarantee in the latter case is not attainable by any procedure that uses only the inputs.
3. Data

EGFR bioactivity data were taken from ChEMBL (Gaulton et al., 2012) in the form distributed with the TeachOpenCADD teaching platform (Sydow et al., 2019; CC BY 4.0): 3,884 distinct structures with pIC50 values between 1.6 and 11.4 (mean of duplicate measurements per structure) and 1,444 Bemis–Murcko scaffolds (Bemis and Murcko, 1996). The ChEMBL servers were not reachable from the working environment, so the GitHub copy of the talktorial data was used.
4. Method

Predictor. Molecules are encoded as Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2,048 bits; Rogers and Hahn, 2010) and a random forest of 200 trees with a minimum leaf size of 2 predicts pIC50 (Breiman, 2001). It stands in for the platform's predictor, which is not part of this study; the uncertainty layer does not depend on it.

Splits. Molecules are divided 60/20/20 into training, calibration and test parts, either at random or by scaffold. In the scaffold split, whole scaffold groups, in random order, are assigned to the parts, so that test molecules belong to chemical series that were absent from training and calibration (chemical-series shift). Ten random seeds are used for each split type.

Intervals. The nonconformity score is the absolute error on the calibration molecules. The global interval has the half-width given by the conformal quantile at level 0.90 of all calibration scores. The Mondrian interval uses a separate quantile for each tercile of the predicted value, estimated from the calibration predictions (a stratum with fewer than 30 calibration molecules falls back to the global quantile).

Metrics. We report the empirical coverage on the test molecules, the coverage within each tercile of the predicted value and the minimum of these (worst stratum), the coverage within three groups of the true activity (pIC50 below 6, between 6 and 8, and above 8; weak, medium and potent) and the minimum of these, and the mean interval width. Results are averages over seeds with 95% t-intervals.
5. Results

The marginal guarantee held under both split types. The Mondrian variant gave no measurable gain. Coverage conditional on the true activity was lower for both variants and was lowest for scaffold splits.
Table 1. Conformal coverage for EGFR (nominal 0.90; mean ± 95% interval over 10 seeds).
6. Discussion and limitations

The central finding is reassuring on one point and cautionary on another. Reassuring: the marginal coverage stayed at the nominal level even when whole scaffolds were held out. That is better than one might fear, and it suggests that, for this target and predictor, the absolute-error distribution on molecules from new scaffolds is close to that on molecules from known scaffolds. A possible reason is that the scaffold split with random group order still leaves related molecules in training (different scaffolds can have similar substituents and activities), so the shift is moderate.

Cautionary: the intervals are about 2.8 pIC50 units wide, that is, about two orders of magnitude in potency, and they cover 78% to 84% of the molecules in the worst activity group. Because the intervals are valid on average over the data, they must over-cover the molecules that are easy to predict (those near the mean activity) and under-cover those at the extremes; the very potent molecules that a chemist is looking for are exactly the ones that are least well covered. Stratifying by the predicted value did not repair this, because the predictor shrinks towards the mean and the predicted value is therefore a poor proxy for the true activity. Claims of the form that a molecule predicted to be potent has a potency within the interval with 90% probability should not be made on the basis of marginal intervals.

Limits of the study. The study uses one target and a random-forest stand-in for the platform's predictor; a second target and the platform's own predictor were not evaluated. Fingerprint type and model were not varied. The scaffold split holds out scaffolds but not other forms of series shift, such as temporal splits that mimic a medicinal chemistry campaign. Duplicate measurements were averaged, which hides assay noise.
7. Conclusion

For EGFR in ChEMBL, split-conformal intervals around a black-box affinity predictor kept their nominal 0.90 coverage under random and scaffold splits (0.896 and 0.894). Mondrian calibration by predicted value gave no gain, and coverage within activity groups was weaker (worst group 0.83 and 0.78) and the intervals were wide. Marginal conformal intervals are a sound way to report reliability on average but should not be read as activity-conditional guarantees.
Implementation and reproducibility

The experiment is implemented in research/s_iqim_hqca (conformal intervals, scaffold and random splits, and the EGFR experiment), added to the drug-discovery platform repository with continuous integration. Six unit tests on synthetic data check the interval logic and the data handling. The result file holds the numbers of Table 1.
Data and code availability

The ChEMBL-derived EGFR data are public (CC BY 4.0 through TeachOpenCADD; ChEMBL itself is CC BY-SA 3.0). The code and result files are in the author's private repository (research/s_iqim_hqca) and are available on request.

blocks.x: A Conservative Lower Bound on Remaining Useful Life as an Add-On to an Asset Life-Cycle Digital Twin: Evidence from NASA IMS Bearing Data
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Digital twins of industrial assets use remaining useful life (RUL) estimates to plan maintenance, but an optimistic estimate can postpone maintenance past failure. We study a lower bound on RUL as an add-on that is separate from the twin: it takes the twin's point estimate and subtracts a calibrated one-sided error quantile, so that maintenance can be planned on a conservative value. The point estimate maps a label-free vibration health index to RUL with a monotone regression; the quantile comes from leave-one-bearing-out predictions on the training bearings. We evaluated the add-on on the four bearings that failed in the public NASA IMS run-to-failure experiments, holding out one failed bearing at a time. The share of overestimating (unsafe) predictions fell from 0.48 for the point estimate to 0.18 for the lower bound, and in the last 48 hours before failure from 0.66 to zero; a constant-life baseline overestimated in 0.75 of all cases. The price was premature alerts: the share of snapshots with an alert more than 192 hours before failure rose from zero to 0.23, mostly on the longest-lived bearing, whose lower bound was low from the start. With only four failed bearings the results are preliminary and the intervals are wide. The method needs no failure labels from the monitored machine and can run on industrial edge hardware.
Keywords: digital twin; remaining useful life; predictive maintenance; conservative bound; condition monitoring
1. Introduction

A digital twin of an industrial asset is useful for maintenance only if it tells the planner when to act. Its most important output is the remaining useful life (RUL), the time until the asset reaches a failure threshold. A planner who acts on a RUL estimate that is too optimistic lets the asset run on, and the failure arrives before the maintenance does; an estimate that is too pessimistic causes premature replacement and loss of useful life. The costs of the two errors are not symmetric. For critical rotating machinery, an unplanned failure is typically far more expensive than a planned intervention, so a conservative estimate is preferred.

Most RUL models return a point estimate. Turning it into a conservative value requires knowing how large its errors are, and for a data-driven model the errors are not known until the asset has failed. Run-to-failure data are scarce: each failure is an event that operators work hard to avoid. This paper proposes a simple add-on that is separate from the twin itself. It takes the twin's point estimate and subtracts a one-sided error allowance, calibrated on the training assets by leave-one-asset-out predictions, so that maintenance can be planned on a lower bound of RUL. Because it uses only the output of the twin, it does not require access to the twin's internals, and because the health indicator it builds on is derived from the vibration signal alone, it needs no failure labels from the monitored machine.

We evaluate the add-on on the public NASA IMS bearing experiments, which contain four run-to-failure bearings. The data are few, and the paper's claims are limited accordingly. The question is whether the lower bound reduces the share of dangerous (overestimating) predictions, and what it costs in premature alerts.
2. Related work

Prognostics and health management has a large literature, reviewed for machinery by Lei et al. (2018) and for the field as a whole by Zio (2022). Benchmark data sets include the turbofan simulations of C-MAPSS (Saxena et al., 2008) and the bearing experiments of the IMS centre (Lee et al., 2007; Qiu et al., 2006). Uncertainty-aware RUL estimation has been studied with Bayesian methods, ensembles and conformal prediction; conformal intervals for RUL on turbofan data have been published, so interval methods for RUL are not new. Our searches did not find a study that evaluates a conformal-style lower bound on the IMS bearings with leave-one-bearing-out calibration, but the search was not exhaustive.

The add-on is a form of conformalised one-sided bound. The error quantile is estimated from predictions on held-out assets, which is the correct unit of exchangeability for a fleet: a new asset must be exchangeable with other assets, not with other time points of the same asset. This is the same principle as subject-wise splitting in clinical machine learning.
3. Data

The IMS bearing data come from three run-to-failure experiments in which four bearings on a loaded shaft ran until failure, with vibration recorded at intervals of ten minutes (Lee et al., 2007). Four bearings failed: bearing 3 and bearing 4 of test 1, bearing 1 of test 2 and bearing 3 of test 3. We use feature tables extracted from the raw signals (root-mean-square, kurtosis and peak-to-peak values for each snapshot) that are available in a public repository under the MIT licence. Operating time is computed as the cumulative time, in which gaps longer than 15 minutes (pauses of the experiment) count as one ten-minute interval, following the data documentation. The lives of the four bearings were 345, 345, 164 and 1,053 hours.
4. Method

Health index. For each bearing the health index is the logarithm of the root-mean-square value relative to the median of the first 10% of its life, smoothed by a rolling median over 15 snapshots. It uses no failure information.

Point estimate. A monotone (non-increasing) isotonic regression (Robertson et al., 1988) maps the health index to RUL in hours; it is fitted on the pooled snapshots of the training bearings. As a naive baseline, the constant-life model predicts the mean training life minus the age.

Lower bound. The error allowance is the (1 - alpha) quantile, with alpha = 0.1, of the overestimation (prediction minus truth) in leave-one-bearing-out predictions made on the training bearings, truncated at zero. The lower bound is the point estimate minus the allowance, truncated at zero.

Evaluation. We hold out one failed bearing at a time, build the model on the other three and evaluate on the held-out bearing. A prediction is unsafe if it exceeds the true RUL (an overestimate). We report the share of unsafe snapshots over the whole life and over the last 48 hours, the lead time (the true RUL at the first snapshot at which the predicted RUL is at or below 48 hours), and the share of snapshots with a premature alert, that is, a predicted RUL at or below 48 hours when the true RUL is above 192 hours.
5. Results

Table 1 summarises the results averaged over the four held-out bearings. The point estimate overestimated the RUL in 0.48 of the snapshots and in 0.66 of the snapshots in the last 48 hours. The lower bound reduced these shares to 0.18 and zero. The constant-life baseline overestimated in 0.75 of all snapshots. The price of the lower bound was premature alerts: the share of snapshots with an alert more than 192 hours before failure rose from zero to 0.23.
Table 1. Mean over the four held-out bearings (NASA IMS).

The premature alerts were concentrated on the longest-lived bearing (test 3, bearing 3, life 1,053 hours), where the share was 0.81 and the lower bound raised an alert from the first snapshot, because the allowance (184 hours) was large compared with the health-index-based estimate early in life. On the other bearings the shares were 0.00, 0.11 and 0.00. For the bearings with lives of 345 hours (two bearings) the allowances were 122 and 115 hours, and for the bearing with a life of 164 hours the allowance was 144 hours, so the lower bound was close to zero for most of the short-lived bearing's life and its unsafe share (0.55) remained the highest of the four.
6. Discussion and limitations

The lower bound does what it is designed to do: it removes the dangerous overestimates, in particular in the last two days of life, where a late warning is most costly. The point estimate overestimated in two thirds of the final 48 hours, which means that a planner trusting it would, in that period, more often be told that there is more time than there is. The cost is not hidden: a lower bound that is low early in life gives alerts earlier than needed, and it did so on the longest-lived bearing so strongly that the alert was effectively permanent. This is the expected trade-off of a conservative bound, and it shows the main weakness of a single, constant allowance. The error of a RUL estimate depends on the life of the asset: a bearing that lasts 1,000 hours has larger absolute errors than one that lasts 150. An allowance proportional to the estimate, or one that shrinks as the health index rises, should be tested.

Four failed bearings are too few to say more. The leave-one-bearing-out allowances are estimated from three bearings, with lives ranging over a factor of six; the intervals are wide and the results should be considered preliminary. The calibration unit is the bearing, so the effective sample size is three for each allowance. A fleet with dozens of failures would give a much better-founded allowance.

Limits of the study. The data are laboratory run-to-failure experiments under constant load and speed, with the same bearing type; real assets operate under varying conditions. The health index uses a single feature, the root-mean-square value; kurtosis and peak-to-peak values were available but not used. The point estimator is deliberately simple, and the add-on was not tested with a more accurate estimator. The twin itself is not part of this study: no function of the asset life-cycle digital twin is implemented or disclosed here.
7. Conclusion

A calibrated lower bound on RUL, built on top of a point estimate with leave-one-bearing-out calibration, reduced the share of overestimating predictions on the NASA IMS bearings from 0.48 to 0.18, and from 0.66 to zero in the last 48 hours before failure, at the cost of premature alerts (0.23 of the snapshots). With only four failed bearings the results are preliminary. The approach needs no failure labels from the monitored machine and can be run on edge hardware; its main open problem is an allowance that adapts to the asset's life.
Implementation and reproducibility

The add-on is implemented in research/rul_lower_bound of the asset-management repository (health index, isotonic estimator, overestimation quantile, lower bound and evaluation), with five unit tests on synthetic series, continuous integration and a TRL 4 note. The result file results/rul_lower_bound_ims.json lists the per-bearing numbers behind Table 1.
Data and code availability

The IMS data are public (NASA Prognostics Data Repository). The code and result files are in the author's private repository (the add-on in research/rul_lower_bound of the ApexAsset repository) and are available on request.

blocks.x: Population Equity of Pharmacogenomic Panels: How Many Actionable CPIC Alleles Does a European-Designed Panel Miss?
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Pharmacogenomic panels are usually designed with allele frequencies measured in European populations, and their value for other populations is rarely quantified. Using the CPIC guideline data for nine genes and nine population groups, we compute the share of actionable (abnormal-function) alleles that a panel designed from European frequencies would not capture. Such a panel misses about 49% of the abnormal alleles in sub-Saharan African populations and about 47% in East Asian populations, against 19% in Europeans. The analysis uses published frequencies and no individual-level data. The analysis does not cover the gene CYP2D6 with its structural variants, was not verified against individual-level data, reports no sampling-based confidence intervals and includes no group close to the Iranian population. The result shows that panel design needs population-specific frequency data to avoid unequal clinical benefit. The topic is genomic rather than imaging, and its fit with this special issue must be confirmed with the editors before submission.
Keywords: pharmacogenomics; CPIC; population equity; allele frequency; clinical decision support
1. Introduction

Pharmacogenomic testing aims to match the choice and dose of a drug to a patient's genotype. Guidelines of the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) translate star-allele genotypes into predicted phenotypes, such as poor, intermediate or normal metaboliser, and give prescribing recommendations (Relling and Klein, 2011; Caudle et al., 2014). The clinical value of a test depends on which alleles it can detect. A test panel is a finite list of alleles, and the list is chosen using what is known about allele frequencies. Most of that knowledge comes from studies of people of European ancestry, because of the well-documented imbalance in the participants of genomic studies (Popejoy and Fullerton, 2016).

If a panel is designed from European frequencies, alleles that are common in other populations but rare in Europeans may be left out. A patient who carries such an allele would be reported with a normal-function genotype although the allele impairs function, and a drug could be prescribed at a standard dose when a change is recommended. This is a concrete mechanism by which a genomic technology can give unequal benefit to different populations, in line with concerns raised for polygenic risk scores (Martin et al., 2019). The size of the effect for pharmacogenomic panels is, however, rarely quantified in a way that a laboratory can use when it designs a panel.

This paper quantifies it with a transparent calculation that uses only published guideline data. For nine pharmacogenes and nine population groups, we ask what share of the abnormal-function alleles in a population would be missed by a panel that was designed from European allele frequencies. The calculation does not need individual-level data and can be repeated by any laboratory with the CPIC tables.
2. Related work

CPIC publishes, for each gene, the definition of star alleles, the function assigned to each allele and the allele frequencies in major population groups (Relling and Klein, 2011). The frequencies are compiled from published studies and their coverage differs between genes and groups. Studies of the equity of pharmacogenomics have shown that the frequency of actionable variants differs substantially between ancestry groups, and that many of the variants in commercial panels were discovered in European samples. Our searches found several reports of this equity gap and none for a group close to the Iranian population; the search was not exhaustive.

Reference resources such as the 1000 Genomes Project provide genotypes of people from five continental groups (Auton et al., 2015) and can be used to check or extend guideline frequencies, but they do not resolve the structural variation of some genes, notably CYP2D6, which is a limitation of any analysis based on single-nucleotide variants.
3. Data

We use the CPIC guideline tables for nine pharmacogenes, comprising the function assigned to each allele and the allele frequencies in nine population groups, as published by CPIC. No individual-level data are used. An allele is called abnormal-function if CPIC assigns it decreased function, no function or increased function relative to the reference allele.
4. Method

Panel design. For each gene, a panel designed from European frequencies is defined as the set of alleles whose frequency in the European group exceeds a minimum frequency that serves as the inclusion threshold of the panel; the value of the threshold is recorded with the analysis code. Alleles below the threshold in Europeans are not in the panel, whatever their frequency elsewhere.

Missed share. For a given gene and population group, the missed share is the sum of the frequencies of the abnormal-function alleles that are not in the panel, divided by the sum of the frequencies of all abnormal-function alleles in that population. It answers the question: of all the abnormal-function alleles carried in this population, what fraction is invisible to the panel? The missed share is computed for each gene and population group and pooled over the nine genes for each group.

Reporting. We report the pooled missed share for each population group, with the European group as the reference. For Europeans the missed share is not zero, because alleles below the inclusion threshold are rare but not absent.
5. Results

A panel designed from European frequencies missed about 49% of the abnormal-function alleles in sub-Saharan African populations and about 47% in East Asian populations, compared with 19% in Europeans.

The other six population groups were computed in the same analysis; their values are in the result file of the analysis.
6. Discussion and limitations

The size of the gap is large. For two of the largest regions of the world, roughly half of the abnormal-function alleles carried would not be detected by a panel built on European frequencies, as against about one in five in Europeans. A negative test result from such a panel therefore carries much less assurance in these populations, and a laboratory that serves a diverse population should design its panel from population-specific frequencies. The calculation also gives a simple way to prioritise: alleles that contribute most to the missed share in a population are the candidates for addition.

The analysis is deliberately simple, and its results should be read as an order of magnitude. Guideline frequencies are compiled from heterogeneous studies; some groups are represented by few individuals, and a group label such as East Asian combines populations with different allele spectra. The pooled missed share weights genes by the frequencies of their abnormal alleles, so a gene with many common abnormal alleles dominates the result; per-gene results are more informative for panel design.

Limits of the study. The analysis does not cover the gene CYP2D6 with its structural variants, was not verified against individual-level data, reports no sampling-based confidence intervals and includes no group close to the Iranian population. The inclusion threshold of the panel is a modelling choice, and a different threshold would change the absolute values. The topic is genomic rather than imaging, and its fit with the special issue must be confirmed with the editors.
7. Conclusion

A pharmacogenomic panel designed from European allele frequencies misses about half of the abnormal-function alleles in sub-Saharan African and East Asian populations, against about a fifth in Europeans. Panel design needs population-specific frequency data to give equal clinical benefit, and a simple missed-share calculation from published guideline tables can show laboratories where the gap is largest.
Implementation and reproducibility

The calculation is the module research/pgx_equity of the genomics repository (panel design from reference frequencies and missed share), with three unit tests on synthetic frequencies that check the panel rule and the arithmetic. The repository documents the maturity level (TRL 4).

The CPIC tables are public. The analysis code is in the author's private repository and is available on request.

blocks.x: Conformal Forecast Intervals for Crude-Oil Inventories: Weekly US Data as a Proxy for Terminal-Level Monitoring
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Operators of storage terminals need forecasts of inventory with a stated uncertainty, but terminal-level tank data are rarely public. As a proxy we use the weekly US crude-oil inventories of the EIA (1982–2026, 2,300 weeks) and test a ridge-regression forecast of the h-week change with split-conformal prediction intervals at horizons of one to four weeks, with a chronological 60/20/20 split. The ridge model reduced the root-mean-square error relative to persistence by 1.2% at one week and by 3.9% at four weeks, a small gain, and the nominal 90% intervals covered 0.81 of the test weeks at one week and 0.88 at four weeks, so they were too narrow at all horizons and closest to nominal at the longest. The data are national inventories and not tank levels, and the journal is about pipelines, so the fit of the study with the journal is weak. The study uses national weekly inventories and no exogenous drivers or consensus forecasts, so its claims are limited to the proxy setting. It shows that a simple interval forecast gives a modest accuracy gain over persistence, that static conformal calibration under-covers on this series, and it sets a reproducible baseline for terminal-level data.
Keywords: inventory forecasting; conformal prediction; storage terminals; crude oil; uncertainty
1. Introduction

Storage terminals for crude oil and products sit between pipelines, refineries and ships. Their operators must decide when to accept a cargo, when to schedule a transfer and how much tank capacity to keep free, and each of these decisions depends on a forecast of inventory. A point forecast is not enough for such decisions: a planner who knows that the inventory in four weeks is likely to be between two values can hold a safety margin, whereas a planner who only has a single number cannot. Forecast intervals are therefore the quantity that matters operationally.

The data that would be needed to study terminal-level inventory, namely tank levels and movements, are commercially sensitive and are rarely public. A public proxy is the weekly series of US commercial crude-oil stocks published by the Energy Information Administration (EIA). It is national, not terminal-level, and it is driven by refinery runs, imports and exports, but it has a long history, a regular weekly rhythm and the same basic structure: an accumulating stock with inflows and outflows. This paper asks a narrow question on this proxy. Can a simple forecasting model with conformal prediction intervals deliver calibrated 90% intervals at horizons of one to four weeks, and how much does the model gain over the naive forecast that the stock stays where it is?

We deliberately keep the model simple, since our purpose is to establish a transparent baseline for terminal-level monitoring that an operator can reproduce and that a more complex model must beat. The paper contributes (i) a reproducible evaluation of ridge-regression forecasts with split-conformal intervals on 44 years of weekly inventories, (ii) an assessment of how close to nominal the empirical coverage is at each horizon, and (iii) a discussion of what can and cannot be transferred from national inventories to a tank farm.
2. Related work

Forecasting of energy inventories and prices is a mature field, with methods ranging from exponential smoothing and ARIMA models to regression with exogenous drivers and, more recently, machine-learning models (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, 2021). The naive forecast, which repeats the last observation, is a standard benchmark and is hard to beat at short horizons for persistent series. Regularised linear models such as ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970) are a common, robust baseline when many correlated lags are used as predictors.

Prediction intervals for forecasts are usually derived from a parametric error model. Conformal prediction replaces the parametric assumption by an empirical quantile of calibration residuals (Vovk et al., 2005; Lei et al., 2018; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). For time series, exchangeability is violated, and variants have been proposed that weight recent data or adapt the interval online (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Gibbs and Candès, 2021; Barber et al., 2023). Our searches did not find a published study of conformal intervals for the EIA weekly crude inventories, although related work on inventory forecasting exists; the search was not exhaustive.
3. Data

We use the weekly estimates of US commercial crude-oil stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, published by the EIA in the Weekly Petroleum Status Report (EIA, series WCESTUS1). The file used here contains 2,300 weekly observations from 20 August 1982 to 23 October 2026. The data are national inventories, not tank levels, and they are public-domain government statistics.
4. Method

Forecasting model. For each horizon h = 1, 2, 3, 4 weeks a separate ridge regression predicts the change of inventory over h weeks from the last eight weekly values expressed relative to the current value, plus a sine and cosine term of the week of the year. The ridge penalty is chosen by cross-validated search on the training part. The naive benchmark repeats the last observed value, which corresponds to a zero predicted change.

Conformal intervals. The observations are split chronologically into a training part (first 60%), a calibration part (next 20%) and a test part (last 20%, 458 to 459 weeks depending on the horizon). The model is fitted on the training part. The absolute residuals on the calibration part are sorted and the interval half-width is their conformal quantile at level 0.90, which is the ceil((n + 1) x 0.90)-th smallest value. The interval for a test week is the point forecast plus or minus this half-width (Lei et al., 2018). The calibration is static and is not updated in the test part.

Evaluation. On the test part we compute the root-mean-square error of the ridge forecast and of the naive forecast and report the relative reduction of the error. We also compute the empirical coverage, the share of test weeks in which the realised inventory lies inside the interval, and the interval width, for each horizon.
5. Results

Against the naive forecast, the ridge model reduced the root-mean-square error by 1.2% at one week, 2.4% at two weeks, 3.0% at three weeks and 3.9% at four weeks; the gain is small and grows with the horizon. The 90% conformal intervals covered 0.81, 0.84, 0.86 and 0.88 of the test weeks at the four horizons, so they were too narrow at every horizon, least so at four weeks (Table 1).

Table 1. Forecast accuracy and interval coverage of ridge regression with static split-conformal intervals on the weekly US crude-oil inventories (chronological 60/20/20 split; test part 458 to 459 weeks).

The coverage below the nominal level is the expected consequence of applying a calibration made on one period to a later period in a series whose variability changes with time; the intervals were not adapted online. We did not test this explanation separately.
6. Discussion and limitations

The results show that a simple, fully reproducible procedure gives only a modest improvement over persistence on this series (1.2% to 3.9% in root-mean-square error), which is what one would expect for a series that is dominated by persistence at weekly resolution. The more important finding concerns the intervals: with static split-conformal calibration they under-covered (0.81 to 0.88 for a nominal 0.90), so an operator who used them as a 90% safety margin would have been exposed more often than planned. Online adaptation or recalibration is therefore needed before such intervals can be relied on.

The transfer to a terminal is the main open question. A terminal's inventory is driven by scheduled cargoes, pipeline nominations and vessel arrivals, which are partly known in advance; its variability is lumpier and its seasonality is weaker than that of national stocks. A terminal-level forecast should use these known inflows and outflows as predictors, and intervals should be calibrated per tank group. National inventories show only the baseline difficulty of the problem, not its terminal-specific features.

Limits of the study. The study uses national weekly inventories and not tank-level data, and it uses no exogenous drivers such as refinery runs and imports and no consensus forecasts, so its claims are limited to the proxy setting. Only a ridge model was compared with the naive forecast. The calibration was static; online adaptation of the interval might improve coverage in periods of changing variability. The intervals are marginal over the test weeks, and conditional coverage in unusual periods, for example during the 2020 demand collapse, was not examined separately. Finally, the journal is about pipelines, so the topical fit is limited and the editors should be asked whether inventory forecasting for terminals is within scope.
7. Conclusion

A ridge forecast with static split-conformal intervals improved on the naive forecast by 1.2% to 3.9% in root-mean-square error and reached an empirical coverage of 0.81 to 0.88 for a nominal 0.90 at horizons of one to four weeks on the weekly US crude-oil inventories. The procedure is a transparent baseline for terminal-level monitoring, and its under-coverage shows that adaptive calibration is the first thing a terminal-level method must add. Applying it to a terminal requires tank-level data and the scheduled movements of that terminal.
Implementation and reproducibility

The forecasting and interval code is the module research/inv_forecast of the terminals repository (lag matrix, ridge regression, split-conformal intervals and evaluation), with two unit tests on a synthetic series that check the lag construction and the coverage of the intervals on simulated data; they are not used for any reported result. The repository also documents the maturity level of the component (TRL 4).

blocks.x: ReadmitCal: Are 30-Day Readmission Models for Patients with Diabetes Already Calibrated? A Negative Result on 69,990 Patients
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Hospital readmission risk models are used to allocate follow-up resources, and calibration of their probabilities is often recommended. We test whether post-hoc recalibration, overall and within subgroups, improves 30-day readmission models for patients with diabetes. Using the public Diabetes 130-US hospitals data (69,990 patients after keeping the first encounter of each patient and excluding deaths and hospice discharges) with patient-level splits, we trained logistic regression and gradient boosting and compared Platt scaling, isotonic regression and temperature scaling, applied globally and within three age groups, over 10 random splits. The models were already well calibrated before any correction: the expected calibration error was 0.005 for logistic regression and 0.006 for gradient boosting, and no recalibration method lowered it; recalibrating within age groups did not help either (error about 0.009 to 0.010 in every variant). Discrimination was modest, with an AUROC of 0.646 and 0.650. We report this as a negative result: for this data set calibration is not the limiting problem and discrimination is. Temporal validation, subgroups other than age and a comparison with published fairness audits were not carried out. The study indicates that calibration auditing should check first whether a model is already calibrated and gives a reproducible benchmark for health informatics.
Keywords: hospital readmission; calibration; diabetes; negative result; medical informatics
1. Introduction

Hospitals use readmission risk models to decide which patients should receive extra follow-up after discharge. The models return a probability, and the decisions that use them, such as setting a threshold or comparing cost with benefit, treat that probability as meaningful. This requires calibration: of the patients given a predicted risk of 10%, about 10% should be readmitted. Modern classifiers are not always well calibrated (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005; Guo et al., 2017), and post-hoc recalibration with Platt scaling (Platt, 1999), isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002) or temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017) is often recommended before a model is deployed. Calibration may in addition differ between patient groups, so that a model that is calibrated overall is not calibrated for older patients, for example, and recalibration within subgroups has been proposed.

Whether this effort is worthwhile depends on the data. If a model is already well calibrated, recalibration adds complexity and may even harm. We examine the question on the public Diabetes 130-US hospitals data (Strack et al., 2014), a widely used benchmark of readmission among patients with diabetes: are standard 30-day readmission models already calibrated, and does global or subgroup recalibration improve them? We find that they are, and that it does not. The limiting factor is discrimination, not calibration.
2. Related work

Readmission prediction has been studied extensively, with logistic regression, tree ensembles and neural networks on administrative and clinical data, and with generally modest discrimination (area under the ROC curve typically 0.6 to 0.7). The Diabetes 130 data of Strack et al. (2014) contain 101,766 encounters from 130 US hospitals over ten years and are the basis of many studies. Calibration studies on the same data exist in the literature and in open-source projects. Calibration is measured by reliability diagrams, the expected calibration error (Naeini et al., 2015) and the Brier score; our results use the first and last, with a fixed binning.
3. Data

Diabetes 130-US hospitals for years 1999 to 2008 (Strack et al., 2014; Creative Commons Attribution licence): 101,766 hospital encounters with demographic, clinical and treatment variables. We keep the first encounter of each patient, so that the same patient does not appear in more than one split, and exclude encounters that ended in death or discharge to hospice, after which readmission is not possible. This leaves 69,990 patients, of whom 8.98% were readmitted within 30 days. The file used in the analysis was a public GitHub copy of the UCI file (the UCI server was not reachable from the working environment); two GitHub copies were checked and were byte-identical.
4. Method

Features. Eight numeric variables (time in hospital, numbers of laboratory procedures, procedures, medications, outpatient, emergency and inpatient visits, and number of diagnoses), ten categorical variables (race, gender, age group, admission type, discharge disposition, admission source, HbA1c result, change of medication, diabetes medication, maximum glucose serum) and the first three digits of the primary diagnosis code and the medical specialty (each reduced to its 25 most frequent values plus 'other') are used, with one-hot coding and standardisation fitted on the training part.
Models. L2-regularised logistic regression and histogram-based gradient boosting (150 iterations, learning rate 0.05, at most 15 leaves).
Splits. 60/20/20 into training, validation and test patients, repeated for 10 random seeds. Recalibration maps are fitted on the validation part and evaluated on the test part.

Recalibration. Platt scaling, isotonic regression and temperature scaling, each applied globally. For the subgroup analysis, the same three methods are fitted separately within three age groups (up to 60 years, 60 to 80 years and 80 years and older, determined by the age band of the record), and the expected calibration error is computed within each group and averaged.
Metrics. Area under the ROC curve, Brier score and the expected calibration error with 15 equal-width bins; means over seeds with 95% intervals.
5. Results

Both models were already well calibrated before any correction. The expected calibration error was 0.0053 for logistic regression and 0.0061 for gradient boosting, and none of the recalibration methods reduced it. Subgroup recalibration did not help either: the error within age groups was about 0.009 to 0.010 in every variant, with raw predictions about as good as the recalibrated ones. Discrimination was modest, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.646 and 0.650.
Table 1. Discrimination and expected calibration error on 69,990 patients (mean ± 95% interval over 10 seeds; ECE = expected calibration error).
6. Discussion and limitations

An expected calibration error near 0.005 for a base rate of 9% is small, and recalibration changes it by amounts smaller than the seed-to-seed variation. The reason is mechanical: logistic regression optimises the log-loss, so it is calibrated on average by construction when the model is reasonably specified, and gradient boosting with a small learning rate and moderate depth did not over-fit in the way that makes deep networks over-confident. The subgroup result is similar. Fitting separate maps in groups of a few thousand patients added estimation noise without removing a bias that was not there.

The practical message is to test before correcting. A reliability check on a validation set takes minutes, and if the model is already calibrated, effort should go to what limits the value of the model, here its discrimination: an area under the curve of 0.65 means that the model ranks patients only modestly better than chance, and no recalibration can change that.

Limits of the study. Temporal validation, subgroups other than age and a comparison with published fairness audits were not carried out. The first-encounter design excludes repeat admissions, which are the patients at highest risk. The data are from 1999 to 2008 and may not represent current practice. The analysis uses a fixed feature set and two model families; deep models, which are more prone to mis-calibration, were not tested. The expected calibration error depends on the binning, and 15 bins is one choice. The research script has no unit tests; it was verified by re-running it.
7. Conclusion

On 69,990 patients of the Diabetes 130-US hospitals data, 30-day readmission models were already well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.005 to 0.006), and neither global nor age-subgroup recalibration improved them. Discrimination (AUROC 0.646 to 0.650) is the limiting factor. Calibration audits should check first whether recalibration is needed.
Implementation and reproducibility

The experiment is a single script (research/s_mie_readmitcal/run.py) that reads the Diabetes 130 file and writes results.json with every number in Table 1 and the subgroup results; it uses scikit-learn and SciPy. A note in the repository documents the data source and the checks made on the file.
Data and code availability
The Diabetes 130 data are public (UCI, CC BY 4.0). The code and result files are in the author's private repository (research/s_mie_readmitcal) and are available on request.

blocks.x: Random Splits Overstate Wearable Activity Recognition: Per-Subject Accuracy on UCI HAR
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Reported accuracy of wearable activity recognition depends on how the data are split. Using the UCI HAR data of 30 subjects, we compare random window splits with subject-level splits. Random splitting overstated accuracy by 3 to 5 percentage points, and some subjects reached only 72% to 79% accuracy. Conformal prediction intervals kept coverage above 0.9 in both settings, so no leakage effect on coverage was seen. The study is small and its fit with this journal is doubtful. The study uses one data set and classical models; confidence intervals over several seeds were not computed, and deep models and free-living or clinical data were not evaluated. We recommend subject-level evaluation and per-subject reporting for digital-health claims based on wearable sensors.
Keywords: wearable sensors; activity recognition; evaluation protocol; data leakage; digital health
1. Introduction

Smartphones and wearable sensors are used to recognise activities such as walking, sitting and climbing stairs, and the recognised activity is a building block of digital-health applications, from step counting to fall detection and monitoring of rehabilitation. Studies of such systems report accuracy, often high. How that accuracy was measured determines what it means. The data of a wearable study are windows of sensor signal, cut from long recordings of a small number of people. If windows of the same person are used both to train and to test a model, the model can learn the person's own movement signature instead of the activity, and the accuracy it reports does not describe what a new user will experience. This effect is a form of data leakage (Kaufman et al., 2012).

The remedy is to split by subject, so that no person appears in both the training and the test set; this is the cross-validation that matches the use case of a product that is delivered to people it has never seen (Saeb et al., 2017; Roberts et al., 2017). Despite this, random window-level splits remain common, and the size of the effect on a standard benchmark is not always stated. This paper measures it on the public UCI Human Activity Recognition data set (Anguita et al., 2013), and also reports accuracy for each subject, because a mean can hide subjects for whom a system works poorly. We further ask whether conformal prediction sets keep their coverage under the two evaluation protocols.
2. Related work

The UCI HAR data set, recorded by 30 volunteers wearing a smartphone at the waist, is one of the most used benchmarks for activity recognition (Anguita et al., 2013). The data set is distributed with a predefined split by subject into training and test parts, and a large body of work uses it. Several studies have documented that subject-independent evaluation gives lower accuracy than window-level random splitting for wearable data (see, for example, arXiv:2310.11950). The general principle of splitting by the unit that generates the dependence is well established in machine learning and in ecology (Roberts et al., 2017), and in clinical machine learning (Saeb et al., 2017).

Our contribution is modest and practical: a small, reproducible comparison on one standard data set that reports both the average over subjects and the spread between them, and that adds an uncertainty-quantification angle by checking the coverage of conformal prediction intervals under both protocols.
3. Data

We use the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones data set (Anguita et al., 2013): 30 subjects aged 19 to 48 performed six activities (walking, walking upstairs, walking downstairs, sitting, standing and lying) while wearing a waist-mounted smartphone. The signals of the accelerometer and the gyroscope were cut into overlapping windows of 2.56 s at 50 Hz, and 561 features were derived for each window. The data set is public and distributed under a Creative Commons Attribution licence.
4. Method

Two evaluation protocols are compared for the same classifier. In the random protocol, the windows of all subjects are pooled and randomly divided into training and test windows. In the subject protocol, subjects are divided into training and test groups, so that every test window comes from a person who is not in the training set. The two protocols use the same feature set and the same classifier, so the difference in accuracy is due to the protocol and not to the model.

We use classical classifiers on window features. Accuracy is the share of test windows with the correct activity. Under the subject protocol we also compute accuracy for each test subject. Conformal prediction sets are computed with the split method and a nominal coverage of 0.90 under both protocols, and we report the empirical coverage of the sets on the test windows.
The difference between the two protocols is reported as the number of percentage points by which random splitting overstates the accuracy of the subject protocol.
5. Results

Random splitting overstated accuracy by 3 to 5 percentage points relative to subject-level evaluation. Under the subject protocol the accuracy for individual subjects varied substantially: some subjects reached only 72% to 79%. Conformal prediction sets kept the empirical coverage above 0.9 in both settings, so no effect of the leakage on coverage was seen.

6. Discussion and limitations

The overstatement of 3 to 5 percentage points is not dramatic, which is partly because UCI HAR is an easy data set on which accuracies of 90% and more are common, and partly because the six activities are physically very different. The effect is likely to be larger for finer activity classes, for clinical populations whose movement differs strongly from person to person, and for free-living data. The spread between subjects is the more important result for digital-health claims: a system that reaches a high mean accuracy but 72% to 79% for some people may be unacceptable for them, and the mean hides this.

The conformal sets kept their coverage above the nominal level in both protocols. This is expected when the calibration data are drawn with the same protocol as the test data: a calibration set made of random windows is exchangeable with a random test set, and a calibration set made of other subjects is approximately exchangeable with test subjects as long as subjects are drawn from the same population. It is a reminder that the evaluation protocol has to mimic the deployment, since coverage guarantees hold with respect to the way in which calibration and test data are generated.

Limits of the study. The study is small and its fit with this journal is doubtful. It uses one data set and classical models; confidence intervals over several seeds were not computed, and deep models and free-living or clinical data were not evaluated. The 30 volunteers are healthy adults, wearing the phone in one position. Splits by subject with 30 subjects give a limited number of test subjects, so the per-subject range is itself uncertain.
7. Conclusion

On UCI HAR, random window-level splitting overstated the accuracy of activity recognition by 3 to 5 percentage points compared with subject-level evaluation, and some subjects reached only 72% to 79% accuracy. Subject-level evaluation and per-subject reporting should be the default for digital-health claims based on wearable sensors.
Implementation and reproducibility

WearShift is a Python package with a synthetic accelerometer generator that plants user and device effects, window features (mean, standard deviation, energy, zero-crossing rate, dominant and mean frequency per axis and for the magnitude, axis correlations), scenarios for in-distribution, cross-user and cross-device evaluation, a shift statistic, and mitigations (per-domain standardisation, correlation alignment and few-shot calibration). On the synthetic data (10 users) the macro-F1 was 0.994 in distribution, 0.931 for a new user and 0.900 for a new device; this is a check of the code, not a claim about real sensors. The comparison of random and subject-level splits reported here is on the real UCI HAR data.

blocks.x: Conformal Alarm Thresholds for Oil-Well Fault Detection on Real Petrobras 3W Data: A Well-Level Evaluation of False-Alarm Control and Detection
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Fault detection in oil wells must keep false alarms low while still detecting faults. We study a conformal alarm threshold as an add-on to an artificial-lift management system, using the public Petrobras 3W data, version 2: 1,119 real instances from 40 wells (594 normal, 525 faults of nine types). A robust z-score statistic is computed from seven sensors against a reference taken at the start of each instance, and the threshold is the conformal quantile of the maxima of normal calibration instances at a target false-alarm rate of 0.10. Wells were split between calibration and test in 20 random repetitions. The false-alarm rate on unseen wells was 0.147 on average, but ranged from 0.009 to 0.551 between splits and exceeded the target in half of them; fixed thresholds of z = 5, 10 and 20 gave 0.195, 0.103 and 0.067. Hence the instance-level guarantee does not transfer to new wells, because instances of one well are not exchangeable with those of others. From the labelled onset, alarms were raised for 87% and 96% of the instances of two fault types but for only 9% of the 343 instances of the largest class, which these sensors barely reveal. Alarms before the onset cannot be distinguished from false alarms and are not counted as early warning. Calibration by well and fault-specific sensors are needed. The threshold was compared with fixed thresholds only; other detectors such as Isolation Forest or CUSUM were not evaluated.
Keywords: artificial lift; fault detection; conformal prediction; alarm threshold; Petrobras 3W
1. Introduction

Artificial-lift systems such as gas lift, electric submersible pumps and progressive-cavity pumps keep a large share of the world's oil wells producing. Their faults, for example a closed valve, scaling, a hydrate or an abrupt change in productivity index, reduce production and can damage equipment, so operators run alarm systems on pressure, temperature and flow signals. An alarm system has two competing goals. It must keep false alarms low, because operators ignore a system that cries wolf, and it must detect faults early enough to act. A threshold on a statistic of the sensor data sets this trade-off, and the usual way to choose it is by experience or by trial on historical data.

Conformal prediction suggests a principled alternative: choose the threshold as a quantile of the statistic on normal data, so that a normal instance exceeds it with a chosen probability. The guarantee relies on the calibration and test instances being exchangeable. In a field, however, instances come from a limited number of wells, and the instances of one well are more alike than instances of different wells. A new well is therefore not exchangeable with the wells used for calibration, and the false-alarm rate on a new well may be higher than promised.

This paper tests the conformal alarm threshold on real data and at the level that matters operationally: unseen wells. We use the public Petrobras 3W data set, which collects real events from offshore wells, and we ask three questions. Does a conformal threshold calibrated on some wells keep the false-alarm rate on other wells at its target? How much of the labelled fault is detected? And does the alarm come early enough to be useful? The answers are mixed, and we report them as they are.
2. Related work

Fault detection and diagnosis in oil and gas production has been studied with statistical process control, principal-component analysis, and, more recently, supervised and unsupervised machine learning. The 3W data set (Vargas et al., 2019) was released to give the field a realistic public benchmark with rare undesirable events in oil wells; version 2 contains real, simulated and hand-drawn instances, and several studies have used it to compare classifiers. Most of these studies evaluate classification of the event type on windows of data, not the alarm threshold of a detector.

Conformal prediction (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021) has been applied to anomaly detection by setting a threshold on a nonconformity score. When calibration and test data are exchangeable, the false-alarm rate on new normal data is at most the chosen level on average. Extensions treat covariate shift by weighting (Tibshirani et al., 2019) and online shift by adapting the level (Gibbs and Candès, 2021). Whether the instance-level guarantee transfers to new wells, where the unit of exchangeability should arguably be the well, has, to our knowledge, not been tested on the real 3W instances; our searches did not find such a study, but they were not exhaustive.
3. Data

We use version 2 of the Petrobras 3W data set (Vargas et al., 2019), which is released under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Only the real instances are used; simulated and hand-drawn instances are excluded. This leaves 1,119 instances from 40 wells, of which 594 are normal and 525 contain one of nine fault types, with 4, 22, 32, 343, 11, 6, 36, 14 and 57 instances respectively for fault types 1 to 9. The instances have one-minute sampling and seven sensors: downhole pressure (P-PDG), pressure and temperature at the temperature and pressure transducer (P-TPT, T-TPT), pressure upstream of the production choke (P-MON-CKP), temperature downstream of the production choke (T-JUS-CKP), pressure downstream of the gas-lift choke (P-JUS-CKGL) and gas-lift flow rate (QGL). Each fault instance has a labelled onset after which the well is in the fault state; the part before the onset is labelled normal.
4. Method

Statistic. For each instance the first 30 minutes are taken as a reference, since they are labelled normal. Each sensor is smoothed with a rolling median of five minutes and converted to a robust z-score relative to the median and the median absolute deviation of the reference. The instance statistic is the maximum over time and sensors of the absolute robust z-score.

Conformal threshold. The threshold is the conformal quantile at level 1 - alpha, with alpha = 0.10, of the statistics of the normal calibration instances. A normal instance exceeds the threshold with probability at most 0.10 if it is exchangeable with the calibration instances.

Evaluation at the level of wells. The wells are split at random into a calibration half and a test half, so that the test instances belong to wells that were not used for calibration. The split is repeated 20 times. We report the false-alarm rate, that is the share of normal test instances whose statistic exceeds the threshold, its mean, standard deviation and range over the splits, and the share of splits in which it exceeds the target. For comparison we use fixed thresholds of z = 5, 10 and 20 that need no calibration.

Detection. For fault instances we count a detection if the statistic exceeds the threshold at any time from the labelled onset on, and report the share of detected instances for each fault type among the held-out instances. Alarms that occur before the labelled onset cannot be distinguished from false alarms, because that part of the instance is labelled normal, so they are not counted as early warning; we report how often they occur.
5. Results

False-alarm control. With a target of 0.10 the false-alarm rate on unseen wells was 0.147 on average, with a standard deviation of 0.171. Over the 20 splits it ranged from 0.009 to 0.551 (5th to 95th percentile) and it exceeded the target in half of the splits. The fixed thresholds gave 0.195 (z = 5), 0.103 (z = 10) and 0.067 (z = 20).
Table 1. False-alarm rate of the conformal and fixed thresholds on normal instances of wells not used for calibration.

Detection. Table 2 gives the share of held-out fault instances for which the statistic exceeded the conformal threshold from the labelled onset on. Two fault types were detected in 96% (type 2) and 87% (type 8) of the instances, and others in 35% to 74%. The largest class, type 4 with 343 instances, was detected in only 9%.
Table 2. Share of held-out fault instances detected by the conformal threshold (alpha = 0.10).

Alarms before the onset occurred in 4% to 86% of the fault instances, depending on the fault type. Because the pre-onset part is labelled normal, these cannot be told apart from false alarms; they show that some faults are preceded by a drift that the statistic already picks up, but they cannot be credited as warning with the labels that the data set provides.
6. Discussion and limitations

The main finding is negative. The conformal guarantee holds for exchangeable instances; instances of one well are not exchangeable with those of another, and the false-alarm rate on unseen wells was above the target on average and above it in half of the splits, with a range that spans a factor of sixty. A user who calibrates on instances and deploys on a new well gets no reliable false-alarm rate. The fixed threshold of z = 10 gave a similar average rate with no calibration at all, which shows that the conformal procedure, applied in this way, did not add control over the false-alarm rate.

The right design follows from the cause. If the unit of exchangeability is the well, calibration should be done by well: the quantile should be computed over wells (for example over the maximum statistic per well), or the calibration should include data from the new well itself, for instance from its first days of normal operation. We did not test either option here. The detection results show a second limit: a generic statistic on seven sensors detects some faults well and others, such as the large type-4 class, hardly at all. Fault-specific features, sensors or statistics are needed for those types.

Limits of the study. The threshold was compared with fixed thresholds only; other detectors such as Isolation Forest or CUSUM were not evaluated. One statistic and one reference length (30 minutes) were used. The data come from one operator and 40 wells, and the number of instances per fault type is small for several types, so the detection shares of types 1, 5 and 6 rest on 4, 11 and 6 instances. The repeated well-level splits are not independent of each other, so the standard deviation over splits describes the sensitivity to the split rather than a sampling error. Finally, detection was counted from the labelled onset, which makes it a generous measure of timeliness.
7. Conclusion

A conformal alarm threshold calibrated on instances did not keep the false-alarm rate at its target on unseen wells of the real 3W data: the rate was 0.147 on average against a target of 0.10 and varied between 0.009 and 0.551. Fault detection from the labelled onset ranged from 9% for the largest class to 96% for another. Alarm design for oil wells should treat the well as the unit of calibration, and should use fault-specific signals for fault types that a generic statistic cannot see.
Implementation and reproducibility

The experiment is implemented in research/s_pet_intellilift (statistic, conformal threshold, well-level splits and detection) and has also been added to the artificial-lift management repository as a TRL 4 component with continuous integration. Three unit tests on synthetic series check the statistic and the threshold; no synthetic data are used in the results. The result file lists every number in the tables.

The 3W data are public (Petrobras, version 2). The code and result files are in the author's private repository (research/s_pet_intellilift) and are available on request.
