blocks.x: Shot-Budget Allocation for Pauli-Sum Observables: A Simulation Study of Weighted Allocation and Classical Shadows
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Estimating the expectation value of a Hamiltonian on a quantum computer requires many repeated measurements, and the way a fixed budget of shots is divided among the Pauli terms determines the accuracy of the estimate. We compare uniform allocation, allocation weighted by coefficient magnitude and random-Pauli classical shadows at equal total shot budget for the ground states of H2 (4 qubits, 14 Pauli terms) and LiH (12 qubits, 630 terms) in the STO-3G basis. The Hamiltonians are computed with PySCF and OpenFermion and not measured on a device, because no public hardware measurement data set was found. Variances of the term-wise allocations were computed exactly and those of the shadows by Monte Carlo. Relative to uniform allocation, weighting by coefficient magnitude lowered the root-mean-square error by 14% for LiH but raised it by 35% for H2, and classical shadows gave about three times the error of uniform allocation for both molecules. An oracle allocation that uses the unknown state reached 0.57 (LiH) and 0.75 (H2) of the uniform error, and no scheme without grouping reached chemical accuracy (1.6 mHa) for LiH at 10^6 shots (best: 5.9 mHa without the oracle). The poster will show the protocol, this negative result for shadows and the limits of a simulation-only study. Grouping of commuting terms, larger molecules and hardware noise were not evaluated; we make no claim about performance on hardware.
Keywords: shot budget; Pauli observables; classical shadows; measurement allocation; quantum simulation
1. Introduction

A quantum computer estimates the energy of a molecule by measuring the expectation value of its Hamiltonian, which is a sum of many Pauli terms, on a prepared state. Each measurement (a shot) gives a random outcome, so the energy estimate has a statistical error that falls with the square root of the number of shots. Because the number of Pauli terms grows quickly with the size of the molecule (14 terms for H2 in a minimal basis, 630 for LiH), the measurement cost is a major obstacle for variational algorithms (Peruzzo et al., 2014; Wecker et al., 2015). A fixed shot budget has to be allocated among the terms, and the allocation determines the accuracy that the budget buys.

Several allocation schemes exist: uniform allocation, allocation proportional to the coefficient magnitude (Wecker et al., 2015), the optimal allocation that is proportional to the product of the coefficient and the standard deviation of the term (which requires knowledge of the state), and randomised measurement schemes such as classical shadows (Huang et al., 2020). We compare them at equal total budget in a simulation of two small molecules. The study is simulation only and makes no claim about hardware.
2. Related work

Reducing the measurement cost is an active field. Grouping of commuting terms reduces the number of distinct circuits, term-wise allocation with weights reduces the variance for a given number of shots (Wecker et al., 2015), and classical shadows (Huang et al., 2020) give guarantees for the estimation of many observables from randomised measurements. Variance-based and adaptive allocation of shots is well covered in the literature; our searches found that allocation weighted by coefficients or variances has been studied extensively, while the comparison with random-Pauli classical shadows for the full Hamiltonian at equal budget is less covered. We do not claim novelty of the schemes.
3. Data

The Hamiltonians are computed, not measured. The one- and two-electron integrals are computed with PySCF (Sun et al., 2018) in the minimal STO-3G basis and mapped to qubit operators with the Jordan–Wigner transformation in OpenFermion (McClean et al., 2020). H2 at a bond length of 0.74 Å has 4 qubits and 14 Pauli terms; LiH at 1.6 Å has 12 qubits and 630 Pauli terms. The state is the exact ground state, with energies of −1.1373 Ha and −7.8823 Ha, equal to the full-configuration-interaction values. No public hardware measurement data set suitable for this comparison was found.
4. Method

Schemes. Uniform allocation gives each term the same number of shots. Weighted allocation gives each term shots in proportion to the absolute value of its coefficient. The oracle allocation gives shots in proportion to the absolute coefficient times the standard deviation of the term in the state; it needs the unknown state and is a reference only. In all three, one term is measured per shot and no commuting terms are grouped. Classical shadows use random local Pauli measurements of all qubits, and the energy is estimated from the snapshots.

Error. The term-wise estimators are unbiased, so their root-mean-square error (RMSE) is the standard deviation, which is computed analytically from the exact variances. The error of the classical shadows is computed by Monte Carlo, with 200 repetitions for H2 and 60 for LiH, each with 10^4 snapshots, so the shadow numbers are noisy (the LiH bias of 0.025 Ha is about one standard error). We report the RMSE relative to uniform allocation at the same total number of shots; for term-wise schemes this ratio does not depend on the budget because the error falls as the inverse square root of the number of shots.
5. Results

Weighted allocation lowered the RMSE by 14% for LiH but raised it by 35% for H2. The oracle reached 0.57 (LiH) and 0.75 (H2) of the uniform error. Classical shadows gave about three times the error of uniform allocation for both molecules at 10^4 snapshots. In absolute terms, at 10^6 shots the RMSE for LiH was 6.9 mHa for uniform allocation, 5.9 mHa for weighted allocation and 3.9 mHa for the oracle; chemical accuracy (1.6 mHa) was not reached by any scheme without grouping.
Table 1. Root-mean-square error relative to uniform allocation at equal total number of shots (exact ground states, STO-3G).
6. Discussion and limitations

Weighting by coefficient magnitude is not a safe improvement: it helped for LiH and hurt for H2. A plausible reason is that it ignores the state: the variance of a term in the state, not the size of its coefficient alone, determines how many shots it needs, and a term with a large coefficient can be nearly deterministic in the ground state, so that shots spent on it are wasted while small-coefficient terms with large variance are starved. We did not test this explanation term by term. The oracle allocation, which uses the variances, is better than uniform in both molecules, which shows that the knowledge of the state is worth about a factor of 1.3 to 1.8 in error. A practical scheme would estimate the variances from a first batch of shots and allocate the rest adaptively; this was not tested here.

Classical shadows were about three times worse than uniform allocation in this comparison. This is not a contradiction of their guarantees: shadows are designed to estimate many observables from the same data, and for a single Hamiltonian with many weight-high terms the variance of random local Pauli measurements grows with the weight of the term, so they waste snapshots on high-weight terms. Their advantage appears when many different observables are estimated at once.

Limits of the study. The study is simulation only and makes no claim about hardware. Grouping of commuting terms, larger molecules and hardware noise were not evaluated; with grouping, chemical accuracy might be reached. Only two molecules in a minimal basis and one geometry each were used. The shadow results rest on 60 to 200 Monte Carlo repetitions and are noisy.
7. Conclusion

At equal shot budget, weighting Pauli terms by coefficient magnitude changed the error by −14% for LiH and +35% for H2, an oracle allocation reduced it by 25% to 43%, and random-Pauli classical shadows gave about three times the error of uniform allocation. Allocation schemes must be judged on the state, and simple weights are not a safe default.
Implementation and reproducibility

The study is implemented in research/s_qip_shotlab (Hamiltonian construction with PySCF and OpenFermion, the exact variance calculations, the classical-shadow simulation and the evaluation); a TRL 4 scaffold is kept in a separate private repository (articles-qshot-lab). Unit tests on toy two-qubit cases check the variance formulas. The shadow part dominates the run time (about 15 minutes).
Data and code availability

The Hamiltonians are computed with open-source software and the molecular geometries are given in the text. The code and result files are in the author's private repository (research/s_qip_shotlab) and are available on request.

blocks.x: Keeping Emission Prediction Intervals Valid under Drift: Adaptive Conformal Inference on Five Years of Hourly Gas-Turbine Data
Mohammad Parsa Sohrabi · Parsa International Group, Istanbul, Türkiye · Petro Pala Toos · oil.ms.sohrabi@gmail.com
Abstract

Predictive emission monitoring systems estimate NOx and CO from process variables, but their error grows as the plant ages, and an interval that was calibrated once stops being reliable. We use the public UCI gas-turbine data set (36,733 hourly records, 2011 to 2015) and train a gradient-boosting model on 2011–2012, calibrate on 2013 (7,152 records) and test chronologically on 2014–2015 (14,542 records), with a nominal 90% level. The model error for NOx rose from a root-mean-square error of 7.71 in the calibration year to 13.39 in 2015. A split-conformal interval calibrated once covered only 0.644 of NOx records (95% block-bootstrap interval 0.55–0.76) and 0.808 of CO records, with the worst month at 0.06 for NOx. Adaptive conformal inference restored coverage to 0.899 and 0.900, independent of the step size between 0.005 and 0.02, at the price of intervals 30% wider for NOx. A rolling recalibration over the last 1,000 hours reached 0.864 for NOx with a worst month of 0.51. The failure is model dependent: a ridge model had a one-time coverage of 0.926 for NOx but 0.594 for CO. The data come from one turbine at one site, intervals are marginal and not conditional, and no maintenance log was available, so the study shows a monitoring practice rather than a validated emission system.
Keywords: predictive emission monitoring; conformal prediction; distribution shift; gas turbine; condition monitoring
1. Introduction

Gas turbines in power and process plants must report their emissions of nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide. Where continuous emission monitoring hardware is expensive or fails, plants use predictive emission monitoring systems, which estimate the emissions from process variables such as ambient conditions, turbine inlet and exhaust temperatures and compressor discharge pressure (Kaya et al., 2019; Si et al., 2019). The estimate is only useful if it comes with a statement of how far it can be wrong, because that statement decides whether a reading triggers a check, a maintenance action or a regulatory report.

Such a statement is usually produced once, from a calibration period, and then kept. Turbines age, fouling changes the relation between the process variables and the emissions, and the sensors drift, so the error of the model grows while the stated interval stays the same. The question of this paper is simple and operational: on real multi-year data, how much does an interval that was calibrated once lose, and how much of that loss is recovered by methods that update the interval online?

We answer it with split-conformal prediction (Vovk et al., 2005; Lei et al., 2018) as the one-time interval, adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candès, 2021) as the online update, and a plain rolling recalibration as the obvious alternative. The paper contributes (i) a chronological evaluation on 36,733 hourly records over five years, (ii) a comparison of the three calibration modes by overall, yearly and worst-month coverage with block-bootstrap intervals, and (iii) an explicit test of whether the failure depends on the choice of the point model.
2. Related work

Conformal prediction gives distribution-free prediction intervals with finite-sample coverage when the calibration and test data are exchangeable (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021). Time series and drifting processes violate exchangeability, and several remedies have been proposed: weighting of calibration data (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Barber et al., 2023), recalibration with sequential residuals (Xu and Xie, 2021), and online adjustment of the miscoverage level, which is the adaptive conformal inference used here (Gibbs and Candès, 2021; Zaffran et al., 2022).

For gas-turbine emissions, the data set used here was released together with a benchmark of predictive emission monitoring models (Kaya et al., 2019), and neural networks have been applied to cogeneration units (Si et al., 2019). Our searches did not find a published comparison of one-time and online conformal calibration on this data set; the search was not exhaustive.
3. Data

We use the UCI Gas Turbine CO and NOx Emission Data Set (Kaya et al., 2019; licence CC BY 4.0), which contains 36,733 hourly records from a gas turbine for electricity generation for 2011 to 2015 (7,411, 7,628, 7,152, 7,158 and 7,384 records per year). Each record has nine process variables (ambient temperature, pressure and humidity, air filter differential pressure, gas turbine exhaust pressure, turbine inlet temperature, turbine after-temperature, turbine energy yield and compressor discharge pressure) and the two targets, NOx and CO. The data are public, contain no personal information and were used as supplied, without removing any record.
4. Method

Point models. A gradient-boosting regressor with default settings and a ridge regression (penalty 1.0) were fitted separately for NOx and CO on the 15,039 records of 2011 and 2012. No hyper-parameter was tuned on later years.

Calibration and test. The residuals of the 7,152 records of 2013 were used for calibration, and the 14,542 records of 2014 and 2015 form the test part. The order of records was never shuffled. The nominal level is 90%.

Interval modes. (a) Calibrated once: the half-width is the ceil((n + 1) x 0.9)-th smallest absolute residual of the calibration year and is never updated (split-conformal prediction). (b) Adaptive conformal inference: the miscoverage level is updated after each hour by a(t+1) = a(t) + gamma x (0.1 - e(t)), where e(t) is 1 if the observation fell outside its interval; the half-width is the 1 - a(t) quantile of the calibration residuals; step sizes gamma = 0.005, 0.01 and 0.02 were run. (c) Rolling recalibration: the half-width is the conformal quantile of the last 1,000 absolute residuals, which assumes that the true value of each hour is known before the next hour is forecast.

Measures. We report the empirical coverage over the test part, its 95% interval from a moving-block bootstrap (blocks of 500 hours, 2,000 resamples), the mean interval width, the coverage in each test year, and the lowest coverage in any 720-hour block (the worst month).
5. Results

Model error grew over time. For NOx the root-mean-square error of the gradient-boosting model was 3.07 on its own training years, 7.71 in the calibration year, 11.22 in 2014 and 13.39 in 2015 (Table 1). The ridge model did not show this pattern for NOx (error 10.63 in 2013 and 9.70 in 2015), but its CO error rose from 1.53 to 2.94.
Table 1. Root-mean-square error of the point models by year (in the units of the data set).

The interval calibrated once failed where the error grew (Table 2). For the gradient-boosting NOx model it covered 0.644 of the test hours (95% interval 0.55–0.76), 0.74 in 2014 and 0.55 in 2015, and its worst month covered 0.06. For the gradient-boosting CO model coverage was 0.808. Adaptive conformal inference brought the overall coverage to 0.899 for NOx and 0.900 for CO, in both test years, with a worst month of 0.88 and 0.88. The mean width of the NOx interval increased from 24.06 to 31.34.
Table 2. Coverage of 90% prediction intervals on the test years 2014–2015 (chronological test; intervals by moving-block bootstrap).

For the gradient-boosting models the rolling recalibration did better than the one-time interval but not as well as the adaptive method: its coverage was 0.864 for NOx and 0.882 for CO, with a worst month of 0.51 and 0.76, and with intervals that were wider than those of the adaptive method.
The adaptive result did not depend on the step size (Table 3): coverage was between 0.899 and 0.900 for the three values and the width changed by less than 4%.
Table 3. Coverage / mean width of adaptive conformal inference for the gradient-boosting models by step size.

The failure of the one-time interval depended on the point model. With the ridge model the one-time NOx interval covered 0.926 (95% interval 0.90–0.96), close to the nominal level, whereas the one-time CO interval covered 0.594, and only 0.39 in 2015. Adaptive conformal inference gave 0.900 and 0.900 for these two cases.
6. Discussion and limitations

The main result is practical: a calibration made on one year cannot be assumed to hold for the next, and the loss can be large (0.644 against 0.9 for NOx with a model that fitted its training years well). Updating the interval online restored the nominal level in every one of the four model and target combinations at a cost in width, and the choice of the step size was not critical in the range tested. A plant operator can therefore treat the online update as a low-effort safeguard, but should also monitor the observed coverage itself, which this procedure makes possible because the miss indicator is computed for every hour.

Two observations limit the interpretation. First, the ridge model for NOx was not harmed by the one-time calibration, so drift in the interval is a property of the combination of model and process and not of the data set alone. Second, the gradient-boosting model reached an error of 3.07 on its training years and 7.71 in the next year, which indicates that most of the increase is a failure of the model to carry over to a new period, and the adaptive interval handles its symptom, the interval, and not its cause. A retraining policy remains necessary.

Limits of the study. The data come from one turbine at one site, and the hourly records are aggregates. The intervals are marginal over the test hours; conditional coverage, for example at low load or during start-up, was not examined. The adaptive guarantee is a long-run average and does not apply to a short window, as the worst-month values show. The rolling recalibration needs the true emission of each hour to be known immediately, which a monitoring system without a reference analyser does not have, whereas the adaptive method needs the same feedback; in practice both depend on occasional reference measurements, and we did not study sparse feedback. No maintenance log was available, so we could not attribute the drift to a cause. The models were not tuned, and a tuned model might drift less.
7. Conclusion

On five years of hourly gas-turbine data, a conformal interval calibrated once covered between 0.64 and 0.81 of the test hours for a nominal 0.90 with the gradient-boosting models, while adaptive conformal inference kept it at 0.899 to 0.900 for all four model and target combinations, with intervals 30% wider for NOx and 12% wider for CO (gradient boosting). For the gradient-boosting models a rolling recalibration was an intermediate solution. The finding is a monitoring practice, an interval that is updated and whose coverage is tracked, and not a validated emission system; confirming it requires data from several turbines and a reference analyser.
Implementation and reproducibility

The study is implemented in the module research/gt_drift of the gas-turbine digital-twin repository (aci.py with the three interval modes and run_real.py with the evaluation), with four unit tests on synthetic streams that check the logic of the interval modes; they are not used for any reported result. Every number in Tables 1 to 3 is written by run_real.py to results_real.json. The repository documents the maturity level of the component (TRL 4).
